evidence: Pablo's adoption of the Hohner melodica, an instrument distributed through Jamaican schools as a teaching aid, is described across reggae histories and interviews. 'Java', voted the top instrumental of 1972 in Jamaica, is the record that established it as a lead voice rather than a novelty. Held at consensus because no first-hand source is named here (Q22).

earlier.title: the Melodica, sold as a school instrument

trackPair.whatToListenFor: Listen to where each note starts and stops. There is no sustain to lean on, so every note has to be blown and then released, and you can hear him running out of breath and taking more. That is why a plastic school instrument sounds like a person rather than a keyboard. The tone itself is thin and reedy, almost weak, and playing it slowly in a minor key is what turns that weakness into the mood.

explanation: The melodica was made for classrooms, and it was already fourteen years old when Pablo picked it up. He played it slowly, in minor keys, with heavy echo on it, and because you have to blow every note, the phrasing follows breathing rather than fingers. That is what makes it sound human. He called the result the Far East sound and built a whole run of records on it. It shows that a new sound does not need new technology: what changed was the range he played in, the tempo, the tuning and the echo it ran through. The Far East sound is about context, not invention.
